title: A Copy That Was Not a Copy: Implicit Sharing, and the Innocent Read That Makes a Real One

questions.question: A handler reads a QByteArray with b[0] on a local copy of a frame, writing nothing. What does it cost?
options: A full copy of the bytes
questions.explanation: On a non-const array operator[] is the version that can write, so it detaches first. b.at(0) and b.constData() did not copy.

questions.question: What does a copy of a QByteArray cost until one of the copies is written to?
questions.explanation: They share the bytes, and the writer takes its own copy. After b = a the two had the same bytes.

questions.question: Which of b[0], b.at(0), b.data(), b.constData() and b.size() copied the bytes of a shared array?
options: b[0] and b.data(), the ones that can write
questions.explanation: Qt decides by whether the object is const, not by what the code does.

questions.question: 1000 frames are read by a range-for, 4096 bytes each. How many copies through a non-const array and through std::as_const?
questions.explanation: The loop's begin() is the writing version on a non-const array.

questions.question: Why does with_marker take the frame by value?
options: It gets a shared copy that detaches on the first write
It is faster than a reference
questions.explanation: There is exactly one copy and the caller's frame is untouched. The result's first byte was 77 and the caller's still 0.

questions.question: What does the lesson not claim?
options: That the detail is the same in every Qt version
questions.explanation: It is the behaviour of Qt 6.2 as measured, and other versions may differ. Qt 6 made some old pitfalls disappear.
